title: Exploring Life on Earth
subject: Science
description: Comprehensive practice on plant parts, roots, photosynthesis and transpiration, plant products, types of plants, and how plants adapt to plains, mountains, deserts, marshes, coasts, grasslands, forests and aquatic habitats.

questions.question: What are the two main parts of a plant?
questions.explanation: Every plant has two main parts: the root, which grows underground, and the shoot, which includes the stem, leaves, flowers and fruits above the ground.

questions.question: Which part of the plant anchors it in the soil?
questions.explanation: The root anchors the plant firmly in the soil and also absorbs water and minerals for it.

questions.question: The shoot system of a plant includes all of these EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The shoot system includes stems, leaves, flowers and fruits. The root is part of the root system, not the shoot system.

questions.question: Which part of the plant prepares food using sunlight?
questions.explanation: Leaves are generally green due to chlorophyll and use sunlight to prepare food for the plant through photosynthesis.

questions.question: Why are leaves usually green in colour?
questions.explanation: Leaves contain a green pigment called chlorophyll, which captures sunlight and gives leaves their green colour.

questions.question: The process by which leaves prepare food is called photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis is the process by which green leaves use sunlight, chlorophyll, air and water to make food.

questions.question: Which of these root crops stores food in its root?
questions.explanation: Carrots and beetroots are examples of roots that store food for the plant, unlike rose, grass or mango roots.

questions.question: What is the main function of the stem?
options: To support the plant and carry water and food
questions.explanation: The stem supports the plant and transports water and nutrients between the roots and the leaves.

questions.question: Which plant is well known for storing food in its stem?
questions.explanation: Sugarcane has a stem that stores large amounts of food (sugar), unlike rose, pea or lotus stems.

questions.question: What do flowers develop into after they are pollinated?
questions.explanation: Flowers develop into fruits, which contain seeds that can grow into new plants.

questions.question: A tomato plant's flowers eventually turn into tomatoes. What do tomatoes contain?
questions.explanation: Fruits like tomatoes develop from flowers and contain seeds that can grow into new tomato plants.

questions.question: Roots help prevent soil erosion by holding soil particles together.
questions.explanation: Roots bind soil particles together, which is important for maintaining healthy soil in gardens and farms and preventing erosion.

questions.question: Select ALL the functions of a plant's root.
questions.explanation: Roots anchor the plant, absorb water and minerals, and help prevent soil erosion. Making food using sunlight is the job of leaves, not roots.

questions.question: A gardener notices a plant's leaves are yellowing and it looks weak, even though it gets plenty of water. What is the MOST likely reason if the plant is kept in a shady corner?
options: It cannot make enough food without sunlight
questions.explanation: Without enough sunlight, leaves cannot photosynthesise properly, so the plant cannot make enough food and becomes weak, even with adequate water.

questions.question: All plants store food only in their roots.
questions.explanation: Different plants store food in different parts: carrots store food in roots, sugarcane stores food in its stem, and some plants store food in leaves or seeds.

questions.question: Which part of the plant contains the seeds for growing new plants?
questions.explanation: Fruits develop from flowers and contain the seeds that can grow into new plants.

questions.question: Why is the root and shoot division important for a plant's survival?
options: The root only decorates the plant
The root system nourishes the plant while the shoot system helps it grow, reproduce and make food
Roots and shoots do the exact same job
questions.explanation: The root system anchors the plant and absorbs water/nutrients, while the shoot system (stem, leaves, flowers) supports growth, food-making and reproduction — together they keep the plant alive.

questions.question: A rock is matter, but a plant's shadow is not, because a shadow has no mass and takes up no space.
questions.explanation: This distinguishes real plant parts (which are matter) from a shadow, which has no mass or volume and so is not matter — though this fact is more general than plant biology, it helps sharpen the idea of what a 'part' truly is.

questions.question: Which of these best describes the root's job regarding water?
options: It releases water into the air
It absorbs water and minerals from the soil
It stores water only in flowers
It has no role with water
questions.explanation: Roots absorb water and dissolved minerals from the soil and send them up through the stem to the rest of the plant.

questions.question: If a plant's stem is damaged so that water can no longer travel upward, what would you expect to happen to its leaves?
options: The leaves would wilt from lack of water
The leaves would turn into flowers
questions.explanation: The stem transports water and nutrients from the roots to the leaves. If this transport is blocked, the leaves cannot get water and will wilt.

questions.question: Which plant part usually develops seeds that grow into new plants?
questions.explanation: Flowers develop into fruits, and fruits carry the seeds that grow into new plants.

questions.question: What is a habitat?
options: The place where a plant or organism lives
questions.explanation: A habitat is the natural place where a plant or organism lives, such as a desert, forest, or pond.

questions.question: Plants exist in diverse environments like deserts, forests and mountains, and each habitat supports different kinds of plants.
questions.explanation: Different habitats have different conditions (water, temperature, soil), so they support different types of plants adapted to those conditions.

questions.question: A farmer wants a plant that can hold loose soil together on a slope to prevent it from washing away in rain. Which plant feature should he rely on?
questions.explanation: Roots bind soil particles together, so a plant with a strong, spreading root system helps prevent soil erosion on slopes.

questions.question: Select ALL the plant parts that belong to the 'shoot' system.
questions.explanation: The shoot system is everything above the ground: stem, leaves and flowers (and fruits). The root belongs to the root system.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a fruit containing seeds?
questions.explanation: A tomato is a fruit that develops from a flower and contains the seeds for growing new tomato plants.

questions.question: Since flowers are colourful and attractive, they never play a functional role in the plant's life cycle.
questions.explanation: Flowers are not just decorative — they develop into fruits that carry seeds, which is essential for the plant to reproduce.

questions.question: Which of these correctly matches a plant part with its main job?
options: Stem — supports the plant and transports water/food
Flower — anchors the plant in soil
questions.explanation: The stem supports the plant and transports water and nutrients. Leaves make food, roots absorb water, and flowers develop into fruits — not the other way around.

questions.question: Why might a plant with damaged or removed roots eventually die, even if its leaves and stem look healthy?
options: Because roots absorb the water and minerals the plant needs to survive
Because roots make all the plant's food
questions.explanation: Roots absorb the water and minerals needed by the whole plant. Without functioning roots, the plant cannot get water, so it will eventually die despite healthy-looking leaves and stem.

questions.question: Which basic plant part list is correct?
questions.explanation: The basic parts of a flowering plant are the root, stem, leaf, flower and fruit.

questions.question: How many main types of roots are there?
questions.explanation: There are two main types of roots: tap roots and fibrous roots.

questions.question: Which type of root has one main thick root with smaller roots branching off it?
questions.explanation: A tap root has one main, thick root that grows deep into the soil, with smaller roots branching off it.

questions.question: Which plants are examples of tap roots?
questions.explanation: Radish and mango trees have tap roots — a single main root that grows deep into the soil.

questions.question: Which type of root has many small roots of about the same size?
questions.explanation: Fibrous roots consist of many small, similar-sized roots that spread out in various directions, rather than one main root.

questions.question: Which of these plants have fibrous roots?
questions.explanation: Rice and wheat plants have fibrous roots — many thin roots of similar size, unlike the single tap root of carrot, radish or mango.

questions.question: Which plant stores food in its root?
questions.explanation: Carrot has a tap root that stores food for the plant, unlike mango, rose or grass roots.

questions.question: Roots perform essential jobs like anchoring plants and absorbing nutrients.
questions.explanation: Roots are crucial for a plant's stability (anchoring) and nourishment (absorbing water and nutrients).

questions.question: A farmer grows both carrot and grass in his field. While harvesting, he finds it easier to pull out grass than carrot. Why?
options: Grass has no roots at all
Grass has fibrous roots that spread near the surface, while carrot has a deep tap root firmly fixed in soil
Grass roots are heavier than carrot roots
questions.explanation: Fibrous roots (like grass) spread widely near the surface and come out easily, while a tap root (like carrot) goes deep and holds on firmly, making it harder to pull out.

questions.question: Which trees have special 'prop roots' that grow from their branches down into the soil?
questions.explanation: Banyan trees have prop roots that grow from their branches into the soil, allowing a single tree to spread widely.

questions.question: Prop roots allow a single banyan tree to spread widely by giving extra support as it grows outward.
questions.explanation: Prop roots grow down from banyan branches into the soil, acting like extra trunks that help support the tree's wide spread.

questions.question: Which trees have special breathing roots that rise above the soil?
questions.explanation: Mangrove trees have breathing roots that rise above the waterlogged soil to take in air, helping them survive in places like the Sundarbans.

questions.question: Why do mangrove trees need special breathing roots?
options: Because they grow in dry deserts
Because they grow in waterlogged soil where oxygen is scarce
Because their leaves are too heavy
questions.explanation: Mangroves grow in waterlogged soil, which has very little oxygen. Their roots rise above the soil to take in air directly.

questions.question: Root systems can vary significantly depending on the plant type and environment.
questions.explanation: Different plants and environments call for different kinds of roots — from tap roots and fibrous roots to prop roots and breathing roots.

questions.question: The __________ fixes the plant in the soil and absorbs water.
questions.explanation: The root fixes (anchors) the plant in the soil and absorbs water and minerals.

questions.question: Tap roots have one main __________ root.
questions.explanation: Tap roots have one main thick root that grows deep, with thinner side roots branching off it.

questions.question: Select ALL the plants that have tap roots.
questions.explanation: Radish and mango trees have tap roots. Rice and wheat have fibrous roots instead.

questions.question: Select ALL the plants that have fibrous roots.
questions.explanation: Rice and wheat have fibrous roots (many thin roots). Radish and mango have tap roots (one main thick root).

questions.question: A plant growing in a marshy area has roots coming out above the soil. How does this feature help the plant survive?
options: It helps the plant flower faster
It helps the roots take in air, since marshy soil has very little oxygen
It helps the plant make more fruit
questions.explanation: In marshy, waterlogged soil, oxygen is scarce, so roots that rise above the soil (like mangrove breathing roots) let the plant take in air directly.

questions.question: All roots must always stay completely buried underground to function properly.
questions.explanation: Some roots, like mangrove breathing roots and banyan prop roots, grow above or partly above the ground and are essential to the plant's survival.

questions.question: Roots are not just for anchoring — what else do they do, according to the book?
options: They perform various essential functions and can adapt to different environments
questions.explanation: Roots do more than anchor a plant — they absorb nutrients, store food, prevent soil erosion, and can adapt (like prop or breathing roots) to different environments.

questions.question: Which two roots are given as examples of tap roots in the chapter?
questions.explanation: Radish and mango trees are given as examples of plants with tap roots.

questions.question: What is one key real-life benefit of a plant's roots holding soil particles together?
options: It helps prevent soil erosion in gardens and farms
It reduces the need for water
questions.explanation: Roots hold soil particles together, which helps prevent soil erosion — important for keeping gardens and farms healthy.

questions.question: Mangrove trees survive in waterlogged areas such as which famous Indian region?
questions.explanation: Mangrove trees, with their breathing roots, help them survive in waterlogged areas like the Sundarbans.

questions.question: Fibrous roots consist of many small, similar-sized roots growing in various directions.
questions.explanation: Unlike tap roots (one main thick root), fibrous roots are many thin roots of about the same size, spreading in different directions.

questions.question: Think about this: why might different plants need different root styles?
options: Because different soils, water levels and stability needs favour different root shapes
Because roots have no real function
Because all roots are identical in every plant
Because leaves decide the root type randomly
questions.explanation: Plants growing in different soils and conditions (dry, waterlogged, loose, windy) need different root strategies — deep tap roots for stability, spreading fibrous roots for holding topsoil, or special roots for air and support.

questions.question: Besides anchoring the plant, what else do roots absorb from the soil?
questions.explanation: Roots absorb water and minerals from the soil, which the plant needs to grow and make food.

questions.question: Why are roots like carrot and beetroot valuable to us as food?
options: Because they store food (like sugars and nutrients) that we can eat
Because they are always the tallest part of the plant
questions.explanation: Roots like carrot and beetroot store food for the plant, and this stored food is nutritious, which is why we eat these roots as vegetables.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a root with prop roots?
questions.explanation: The banyan tree is known for its prop roots, which grow from its branches down into the soil.

questions.question: Breathing roots are unique to plants growing in dry, sandy deserts.
questions.explanation: Breathing roots (as in mangroves) are found in plants growing in waterlogged soils, not dry deserts — they help the plant get air where the soil lacks oxygen.

questions.question: What is the key difference between tap roots and fibrous roots?
options: Tap roots have one main thick root; fibrous roots have many thin roots of similar size
Tap roots grow only in water; fibrous roots grow only on land
Tap roots make flowers; fibrous roots make fruit
questions.explanation: A tap root is one main thick root with smaller branches, while fibrous roots are a bundle of many thin, similar-sized roots.

questions.question: Which statement about root adaptation is TRUE?
options: Prop roots and breathing roots show that roots can adapt to different environments beyond simple anchoring
Roots never adapt to their environment
Only leaves can adapt to environments, not roots
All roots look and function identically
questions.explanation: Special roots like banyan's prop roots and mangrove's breathing roots show that roots can adapt their structure to suit different environments.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a type of root mentioned in the chapter?
questions.explanation: 'Petal root' is not a real type of root. The chapter discusses tap roots, fibrous roots, prop roots, and breathing roots.

questions.question: What is photosynthesis?
options: The process by which plants make food using sunlight, air and water
The process by which plants absorb sunlight only
The process by which roots grow deeper
The process by which flowers turn into fruits
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis is how plants make food using sunlight, chlorophyll, air (carbon dioxide) and water.

questions.question: What sugar does photosynthesis produce that gives plants energy?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis produces glucose, a sugar that provides energy for plants to grow.

questions.question: What is transpiration?
options: The absorption of minerals by roots
The release of water vapour from plants through stomata
The making of food by leaves
questions.explanation: Transpiration is the release of water vapour from plants through tiny pores in leaves called stomata.

questions.question: What are stomata?
options: Tiny openings on leaves that control water loss and gas exchange
questions.explanation: Stomata are tiny pores on leaves that open and close to control water loss (transpiration) and gas exchange (like taking in carbon dioxide).

questions.question: Tiny pores on leaves are called __________.
questions.explanation: Stomata are the tiny pores on leaves through which gases and water vapour move in and out.

questions.question: Stomata open and close to balance water retention and photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: Stomata regulate how much water vapour is lost and how much carbon dioxide is taken in, balancing the plant's water needs with its need to photosynthesise.

questions.question: What happens without enough sunlight reaching a plant?
options: Plants cannot perform photosynthesis to make food
questions.explanation: Sunlight is essential for photosynthesis. Without enough sunlight, plants cannot convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose (food).

questions.question: What is chlorophyll?
options: The green pigment in plants that captures energy from sunlight
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll is the green pigment in plant leaves that captures sunlight's energy, playing a critical role in photosynthesis.

questions.question: Why do stomata release water vapour on hot days?
options: To help plants stay cool and prevent wilting
To make the leaves grow larger
questions.explanation: Releasing water vapour through stomata (transpiration) helps cool the plant down, which is especially important on hot days to prevent wilting.

questions.question: Which gas released during photosynthesis is vital for animals and humans to breathe?
questions.explanation: Oxygen is released during photosynthesis and is essential for animals and humans to breathe. Plants are a major source of the oxygen we inhale.

questions.question: If a plant's leaves are covered so they cannot transpire or photosynthesise, the plant may wilt.
questions.explanation: Covering leaves blocks both light for photosynthesis and the release of water vapour through stomata, and this can cause the plant to wilt.

questions.question: A plant kept in a dark room for many days becomes weak. Why?
questions.explanation: Without light, a plant cannot photosynthesise and make its own food, so it becomes weak over time.

questions.question: Which of these is a real-life application of understanding transpiration?
options: Ensuring plants have access to air and light for their health
Keeping plants in the dark permanently
Removing all leaves from a plant
questions.explanation: Since photosynthesis and transpiration both depend on air and light, ensuring plants have access to both is crucial for their health.

questions.question: If leaves are covered and cannot receive sunlight, the plant cannot perform __________.
questions.explanation: Without sunlight reaching the leaves, photosynthesis cannot occur, since sunlight is a key requirement for the process.

questions.question: What four things does photosynthesis require, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants make food using sunlight, chlorophyll, air, and water.

questions.question: Select ALL the things stomata help control.
questions.explanation: Stomata are tiny openings that control water loss (transpiration) and gas exchange (taking in carbon dioxide, releasing oxygen). They have no role in root growth or flower colour.

questions.question: Photosynthesis and transpiration are vital processes that support plant life.
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis makes the plant's food, and transpiration helps regulate water and temperature — together they keep plants healthy and growing.

questions.question: A student says, 'Plants only need water to grow, sunlight does not matter.' Why is this statement incorrect?
options: Because sunlight is essential for photosynthesis, which makes the food a plant needs to grow
Because plants do not need water at all
Because sunlight has nothing to do with plant growth
questions.explanation: Photosynthesis requires sunlight along with water, air and chlorophyll. Without sunlight, a plant cannot make food, no matter how much water it receives.

questions.question: How are trees like natural 'air conditioners' for the environment?
options: They release water vapour and oxygen, helping cool and clean the air
They absorb all sunlight so nothing else gets any
They store food only for themselves
They remove all oxygen from the air
questions.explanation: Through transpiration and photosynthesis, trees release water vapour (which cools the air) and oxygen (which cleans the air), acting like natural air conditioners.

questions.question: How much oxygen can a single large tree produce, according to a fun fact in the chapter?
options: Enough for one person a day
Enough for four people each day
Enough for a hundred people each day
questions.explanation: According to the chapter, a single large tree can produce enough oxygen for four people each day.

questions.question: Forests are sometimes called the 'lungs of Earth' because of their role in oxygen production.
questions.explanation: Forests produce large amounts of oxygen through photosynthesis and help maintain the balance of gases in the atmosphere, earning them the nickname 'lungs of Earth'.

questions.question: Which raw materials does a leaf convert into glucose during photosynthesis?
questions.explanation: During photosynthesis, leaves convert carbon dioxide and water (using sunlight and chlorophyll) into glucose.

questions.question: A gardener wraps a leaf tightly in foil for several days while it is still attached to the plant. What is the most likely effect on that leaf?
options: It will be unable to photosynthesise properly due to lack of light
It will turn into a root
questions.explanation: Wrapping a leaf in foil blocks sunlight, so the leaf cannot carry out photosynthesis properly, which can weaken or damage that part of the plant.

questions.question: What does transpiration help a plant do, besides releasing water vapour?
questions.explanation: Transpiration helps keep plants cool and regulates their water content, contributing to overall plant health.

questions.question: Why is chlorophyll described as playing a 'critical role' in photosynthesis?
options: It captures the sunlight energy needed to convert water and carbon dioxide into food
It only gives leaves their colour with no other function
It replaces the need for water
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll captures the sun's light energy, which powers the chemical reactions that turn water and carbon dioxide into glucose during photosynthesis.

questions.question: Leaves make food using sunlight, air, and water.
questions.explanation: This summarises photosynthesis: leaves use sunlight, air (carbon dioxide) and water, along with chlorophyll, to make food.

questions.question: Planting more trees can help with which of these?
options: Cooling and cleaning the air around us
Blocking all sunlight from reaching the ground
questions.explanation: Trees cool and clean the air through transpiration (releasing water vapour) and photosynthesis (releasing oxygen).

questions.question: Two plants are kept in identical pots with the same water, but Plant A gets full sunlight while Plant B is kept in a dark cupboard. After two weeks, which plant is likely to be healthier, and why?
options: Plant A, because it can photosynthesise and make food
Plant B, because darkness helps roots grow faster
Both equally healthy, since water is all that matters
Plant B, because it needs less water in the dark
questions.explanation: Sunlight is essential for photosynthesis. Plant A can make its own food and thrive, while Plant B, lacking light, cannot photosynthesise and will weaken over time.

questions.question: Which of these best defines transpiration in one sentence?
options: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from leaves
Transpiration is the making of food by leaves
Transpiration is the anchoring of a plant by roots
Transpiration is the growth of new flowers
questions.explanation: Transpiration is simply the loss of water vapour from a plant's leaves, mainly through the stomata.

questions.question: Why do stomata need to both open (to release water vapour and take in carbon dioxide) AND close (to conserve water)?
options: Because the plant must balance the need to photosynthesise with the need to avoid drying out
Because stomata are decorative, not functional
Because closing stomata increases sunlight capture
questions.explanation: Stomata must balance two needs: staying open enough to let in carbon dioxide for photosynthesis and release excess water vapour, while closing when needed to prevent the plant from losing too much water and drying out.

questions.question: Which of these products does a plant give us for cooking?
questions.explanation: Sunflower oil, extracted from sunflower seeds, is used for cooking, showing how plants provide us with food products.

questions.question: Which plant is commonly used for skincare?
questions.explanation: Aloe vera is used for skincare due to its soothing, medicinal properties.

questions.question: Which trees provide wood essential for making furniture and houses?
questions.explanation: Wood from trees like pine and teak is essential for making furniture and houses, and is also used for boats and toys.

questions.question: Which plants give us fibres used to make clothes and ropes?
questions.explanation: Fibres from cotton and jute are used to make clothes and ropes; cotton is a key material in everyday clothing.

questions.question: Which of these plants is known for its healing, medicinal properties, along with aloe vera?
questions.explanation: Tulsi, along with aloe vera, is known for its medicinal, healing properties and has been used in traditional medicine for centuries.

questions.question: Plants provide us with a wide variety of products including food, oils, medicines, wood and fibres.
questions.explanation: Plants give us cereals, oils, fibres, wood, medicines and more, impacting many parts of our daily lives.

questions.question: Why is recycling paper beneficial, according to the chapter?
options: It helps save trees and reduce deforestation
It increases the use of plastic
questions.explanation: Recycling paper helps save trees and reduce deforestation; the chapter notes every ton of recycled paper can save about 17 trees.

questions.question: About how many trees can be saved for every ton of paper recycled?
questions.explanation: According to a fun fact in the chapter, every ton of recycled paper can save about 17 trees.

questions.question: Why are jute bags considered an eco-friendly alternative to plastic bags?
options: Because they last forever and never decompose
Because they are made from petroleum
Because they are always more expensive
questions.explanation: Jute bags are biodegradable, making them an eco-friendly alternative to plastic bags and helping reduce plastic waste.

questions.question: Using jute helps reduce plastic waste in the environment.
questions.explanation: Since jute is a natural, biodegradable fibre, using jute products (like bags) instead of plastic helps cut down on plastic waste.

questions.question: What is a GI tag, as mentioned in relation to Alphonso mangoes from Maharashtra?
options: A label that protects the quality and origin of regional products
A type of fertiliser used on mango trees
A machine used to pick mangoes
A pest that attacks mango trees
questions.explanation: A GI (Geographical Indication) tag protects the quality and origin of regional products, like Alphonso mangoes from Maharashtra known for their rich taste.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of a plant-based fibre?
questions.explanation: Cotton is a natural plant-based fibre used to make clothing.

questions.question: Select ALL the products that come directly from plants.
questions.explanation: Sunflower oil, cotton fibre and aloe vera gel all come from plants. Plastic bags are man-made, typically from petroleum, not plants.

questions.question: Which product from trees is used in making boats, furniture and toys?
questions.explanation: Wood from trees like pine and teak is used to make furniture, houses, boats and toys.

questions.question: A shopper chooses a jute bag instead of a plastic bag at the market to help the environment. What is the best justification for this choice?
options: Jute is biodegradable and reduces plastic waste, unlike plastic which persists in the environment
Plastic bags are made from plants too, so it makes no difference
questions.explanation: Jute is a natural, biodegradable fibre, so choosing jute over plastic reduces long-lasting plastic waste in the environment.

questions.question: Forests are sometimes called the 'lungs of Earth' because they help maintain what?
options: The balance of gases in the atmosphere
The number of animals in a zoo
questions.explanation: Forests help maintain the balance of gases (like oxygen and carbon dioxide) in the atmosphere, earning the nickname 'lungs of Earth'.

questions.question: What impact do plants have on our daily lives, based on the range of products they provide?
options: A very wide impact — from the food we eat to the clothes we wear and medicines we use
A very limited impact, mostly just decoration
No impact at all on modern life
Only an impact on farmers, not city dwellers
questions.explanation: Plants give us cereals, oils, fibres, wood, and medicines, impacting nearly every part of daily life, from food and clothing to shelter and health.

questions.question: Aloe vera and tulsi have been used in traditional medicine for centuries.
questions.explanation: Both aloe vera and tulsi are medicinal plants with healing properties that have been used in traditional medicine for a very long time.

questions.question: Cotton is mainly used to produce which of these?
questions.explanation: Cotton is a fibre plant whose fibres are spun into thread and woven into cloth, making it a key material for clothing.

questions.question: Why might using recycled paper products be a good habit for students to develop?
options: Because it helps save trees and reduce deforestation, protecting forests long-term
Because recycled paper is always shinier
Because it uses more trees than fresh paper
Because it has no environmental effect
questions.explanation: Recycling paper reduces the number of trees that need to be cut down, helping protect forests and reduce deforestation.

questions.question: Which of these best completes: 'Plants give us many products, from ___ to medicines and materials.'
questions.explanation: The chapter states that plants provide many products, from food to medicines and materials.

questions.question: Which of the following would you classify as a medicinal plant?
questions.explanation: Aloe vera is a medicinal plant used for its healing and skincare properties, unlike cotton, pine or jute, which are used for fibre or wood.

questions.question: Since wood comes from trees, using wood products always harms the environment with no possible sustainable use.
questions.explanation: Wood can be used sustainably when trees are responsibly managed and replanted, and practices like recycling paper further reduce environmental impact.

questions.question: What kind of product is jute mainly used to make?
questions.explanation: Jute fibre is commonly used to make bags and ropes, and is a popular eco-friendly alternative to plastic.

questions.question: How do GI tags, like the one for Alphonso mangoes, benefit farmers and consumers?
options: They certify the authentic origin and quality of a regional product
They lower the price of all fruits
They ban the sale of the product outside its region
They are only decorative labels with no legal meaning
questions.explanation: A GI tag certifies that a product genuinely comes from a specific region and meets its known quality standards, protecting both farmers' reputation and consumers' trust.

questions.question: Which product below is used specifically in cooking?
questions.explanation: Sunflower oil is extracted from sunflower seeds and is widely used in cooking.

questions.question: Select ALL the benefits of recycling paper mentioned or implied in the chapter.
questions.explanation: Recycling paper saves trees, reduces deforestation, and helps protect forests. It has nothing to do with increasing plastic waste.

questions.question: Which of these plant products is specifically noted as helping reduce deforestation when reused?
questions.explanation: Recycling paper reduces the demand for fresh wood pulp, helping to save trees and reduce deforestation.

questions.question: Plants are classified into types mainly based on what characteristics?
questions.explanation: Plants are classified into types like herbs, shrubs, trees and climbers based on their size and the nature of their stems.

questions.question: Which type of plant has soft, non-woody stems and lives for a short time?
questions.explanation: Herbs are small plants with soft, green, non-woody stems and usually live for a short time.

questions.question: Which of these are common examples of herbs?
questions.explanation: Mint and coriander are common herbs, known for their soft, non-woody stems and short lifespans, often used in cooking.

questions.question: Which type of plant is medium-sized, with thin, woody stems branching near the ground?
questions.explanation: Shrubs are medium-sized plants, larger than herbs but smaller than trees, with thin woody stems that branch near the ground.

questions.question: Which of these are examples of shrubs?
questions.explanation: Rose and hibiscus are shrubs — medium-sized plants with thin woody stems.

questions.question: Trees are tall plants with a thick woody stem called a __________.
questions.explanation: Trees have a thick, woody trunk, with branches growing high above the ground.

questions.question: Which of these are given as examples of trees?
questions.explanation: Mango and banyan are examples of trees — tall plants with thick woody trunks.

questions.question: Which type of plant has weak stems and needs support to grow upright?
questions.explanation: Climbers have weak stems and need support (like a stick, fence, or another plant) to grow upright.

questions.question: Which of these is a common example of a climber?
questions.explanation: The pea plant is a common climber, using its weak stem to grow upward with the help of a support.

questions.question: Which plant type has weak stems that spread along the ground and usually bear large or heavy fruits?
questions.explanation: Creepers have weak stems that spread along the ground, and they usually bear large or heavy fruits, like pumpkin and watermelon.

questions.question: Which of these are examples of creepers?
questions.explanation: Pumpkin and watermelon are creepers — plants with weak stems that spread along the ground, bearing large fruits.

questions.question: Which of these is another common example of a climber, besides the pea plant?
questions.explanation: The money plant is another common climber, using weak stems that need support to grow upright.

questions.question: A student sees a plant with weak stems growing along the ground and bearing large fruits. What type of plant is it?
questions.explanation: A plant with weak stems that spreads along the ground and bears large fruits is a creeper, like pumpkin or watermelon.

questions.question: A rose plant is classified as a shrub because it is medium-sized with a woody stem.
questions.explanation: A rose plant is medium-sized with a thin, woody stem branching near the ground, which fits the definition of a shrub.

questions.question: How would you tell apart a rose plant (shrub) from a mango tree and a mint plant (herb)?
options: By comparing overall size and how woody/thick the stem is
By checking only the flower colour
By checking only the fruit shape
questions.explanation: Herbs, shrubs and trees are distinguished mainly by size and stem type: herbs have soft small stems, shrubs are medium with thin woody stems, and trees are tall with thick woody trunks.

questions.question: Select ALL the plant types that have WOODY stems.
questions.explanation: Shrubs and trees both have woody stems (thin for shrubs, thick trunks for trees). Herbs have soft, non-woody stems, and climbers have weak stems that need support.

questions.question: Which plant type description matches: 'small plant, soft green stem, short life'?
questions.explanation: This description matches a herb — a small plant with a soft, non-woody stem that lives for a short time.

questions.question: A pea plant and a pumpkin plant both have weak stems, but they are classified differently. What is the key difference between a climber and a creeper?
options: Climbers grow upright using support; creepers spread along the ground
Climbers only grow in water; creepers only grow on mountains
Climbers have thick woody trunks; creepers do not have stems at all
There is no real difference between them
questions.explanation: Both climbers and creepers have weak stems, but climbers (like pea) grow upright using support, while creepers (like pumpkin) spread along the ground instead of climbing.

questions.question: Which plant type is the LARGEST and tallest, with branches growing high above the ground?
questions.explanation: Trees are the tallest of the four plant types, with thick woody trunks and branches high above the ground.

questions.question: Herbs generally live for a shorter time than trees.
questions.explanation: Herbs are small, soft-stemmed plants that usually live for a short time, unlike trees, which can live for many years or even decades.

questions.question: Why do climbers and creepers both need support systems or the ground itself, unlike trees?
options: Because their stems are too weak to stand upright on their own
Because their leaves are too heavy
questions.explanation: Both climbers and creepers have weak stems that cannot support the plant upright on their own, so they either use supports (climbers) or spread along the ground (creepers).

questions.question: Which category best fits sugarcane, a plant with a thick, food-storing stem, but not as tall/woody as a tree?
options: It has features closer to herbs/grasses that store food in stems
questions.explanation: Sugarcane is a grass-like plant with a stem that stores food; while not covered as a separate category here, its stem is a notable exception among herb-like plants for storing food.

questions.question: Which two plants are given as examples for climbers in the book's table?
questions.explanation: The pea plant and money plant are the examples given for climbers in the book's table of plant types.

questions.question: According to the book's table, what do creepers usually bear?
questions.explanation: Creepers usually bear large or heavy fruits, as seen in examples like pumpkin and watermelon.

questions.question: If you found a plant with a thin, woody stem branching close to the ground, standing about waist-high, which type would it most likely be?
questions.explanation: A medium-sized plant with a thin, woody stem branching near the ground fits the description of a shrub, like rose or hibiscus.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs correctly matches a plant type with an example?
questions.explanation: Banyan is correctly matched with 'tree'. Rose is a shrub (not herb), mint is a herb (not shrub), and mango is a tree (not climber).

questions.question: All plants with weak stems are automatically classified as trees.
questions.explanation: Plants with weak stems are classified as climbers (if they grow upright with support) or creepers (if they spread along the ground) — never as trees, which have thick woody trunks.

questions.question: What distinguishes a tree's stem from a shrub's stem?
options: A tree's stem (trunk) is thick, while a shrub's stem is thin
A tree's stem is always green, while a shrub's is always brown
A tree has no stem, only branches
There is no difference between a tree's and a shrub's stem
questions.explanation: Trees have a thick, woody trunk, while shrubs have thinner woody stems that branch closer to the ground.

questions.question: Which type of plant would coriander, used often in cooking, be classified as?
questions.explanation: Coriander is a herb — a small plant with a soft, non-woody stem, commonly used in cooking.

questions.question: Why is classifying plants by size and stem type useful for scientists and gardeners?
options: It helps predict how a plant will grow, whether it needs support, and how to care for it
It has no practical use at all
It only matters for naming competitions
It replaces the need to water plants
questions.explanation: Knowing whether a plant is a herb, shrub, tree, climber or creeper helps predict its growth habit, support needs, and care requirements — useful for gardening and farming.

questions.question: What is 'adaptation' in plants?
options: Special features that allow plants to survive in diverse environments
A kind of root only found in deserts
A method farmers use to plant seeds
questions.explanation: Adaptation refers to special features plants develop, like waxy leaves or spines, that help them survive and thrive in specific habitats.

questions.question: Why do plains typically allow plants to grow without needing special survival features?
options: Because plains never get any rain
Because plains are always freezing cold
questions.explanation: Plains generally have pleasant weather with moderate rainfall and temperature, so plants there don't need extreme adaptations to survive.

questions.question: Which type of tree sheds its leaves during dry seasons to conserve water, as seen in the plains?
questions.explanation: Deciduous trees like teak shed their leaves during dry seasons to conserve water, a key adaptation for plains habitats with seasonal dryness.

questions.question: Which trees remain green all year because they get ample water consistently?
options: Evergreen trees like mango and neem
questions.explanation: Evergreen trees like mango and neem remain green throughout the year because they are adapted to consistently moist environments with ample water.

questions.question: Evergreen trees are adapted to consistently moist environments.
questions.explanation: Evergreen trees like mango and neem stay green all year because they grow where water is consistently available.

questions.question: Which shape do mountain plants like pine and fir typically have, to shed snow easily?
questions.explanation: Mountain plants like pine and fir are cone-shaped, which helps snow slide off easily instead of piling up and breaking branches.

questions.question: What kind of leaves do mountain plants like pine typically have?
questions.explanation: Mountain plants like pine have thin, waxy needle-like leaves, which help conserve water and prevent freezing.

questions.question: How can a pine cone act like a 'weather tool'?
options: It opens in dry conditions and closes in wet ones, protecting seeds
It changes colour to predict rain
It grows bigger only in winter
questions.explanation: Pine cones open in dry conditions (to release seeds for dispersal) and close in wet conditions (to protect seeds), acting like a natural weather-responsive tool.

questions.question: Which desert plant is well known for having spines instead of leaves?
questions.explanation: Cacti have spines instead of leaves, which is a key adaptation to reduce water loss in hot, dry deserts.

questions.question: What is the main reason desert plants like cacti have spines instead of leaves?
options: To reduce water loss and deter animals
questions.explanation: Spines reduce water loss (since spines lose much less water than broad leaves) and also deter thirsty animals from eating the plant.

questions.question: Besides cacti, what adaptation do desert shrubs have to minimize water loss?
questions.explanation: Shrubs in deserts have tiny, waxy leaves, which help minimize water loss and survive harsh desert conditions.

questions.question: Deserts are defined only by high temperatures, so all deserts must be hot.
questions.explanation: Deserts are defined by low rainfall, not just high temperatures — some deserts can be cold, like those in Antarctica.

questions.question: A plant in the desert has spines instead of leaves. What is the main reason?
questions.explanation: Spines reduce the surface area for water loss compared to broad leaves, helping the plant conserve water in the dry desert.

questions.question: What defines a desert, according to the chapter, other than just being hot?
questions.explanation: Deserts are defined by their very low rainfall, not simply by high temperatures — some deserts are actually cold.

questions.question: Which best describes why mountain plants like pine and fir are 'suited for cold mountains'?
options: Their cone shape and needle leaves prevent snow buildup and conserve water
Their flowers bloom only in winter
They have no adaptation, just luck
questions.explanation: The cone shape sheds snow easily and the needle-like waxy leaves reduce water loss and resist freezing, together suiting pine and fir for cold mountain climates.

questions.question: Plains have pleasant weather, allowing plants to grow without special features. Why then do some plains trees, like teak, still shed their leaves?
options: Because plains can still have dry seasons where water conservation matters
Because teak trees never need water
Because teak trees are actually mountain plants
Because shedding leaves has nothing to do with water
questions.explanation: Even in generally pleasant plains, seasonal dry spells occur, so deciduous trees like teak shed their leaves to conserve water during those dry seasons.

questions.question: Select ALL the adaptations that help desert plants survive.
questions.explanation: Spines and tiny waxy leaves both reduce water loss, which helps desert plants survive. Broad thin leaves and floating stems are adaptations for other habitats (forests and water), not deserts.

questions.question: Why do mountain plants have thin, waxy leaves?
options: To conserve water and prevent freezing
questions.explanation: Thin, waxy leaves on mountain plants help conserve water and prevent the leaves from freezing in cold mountain conditions.

questions.question: If you found a plant with a cone shape and needle-like waxy leaves, which habitat would it most likely be adapted for?
questions.explanation: A cone shape (to shed snow) and needle-like waxy leaves (to conserve water and resist freezing) are classic adaptations of cold mountain plants like pine and fir.

questions.question: Adaptation in plants mainly involves what?
options: Special features to survive in different habitats
questions.explanation: Adaptation involves plants developing special features (like waxy leaves, spines, or breathing roots) suited to survive in their particular habitat.

questions.question: Cacti have spines that also help protect them from being eaten by thirsty animals.
questions.explanation: In addition to reducing water loss, cactus spines also deter animals looking for water inside the plant, protecting the cactus.

questions.question: Why might a desert shrub's tiny, waxy leaves be considered a superior adaptation compared to broad leaves in that environment?
options: Tiny waxy leaves lose far less water through transpiration, which matters most in dry places
Tiny leaves make more food than broad leaves
Tiny leaves are heavier and shade the roots
questions.explanation: Broad leaves have a large surface area that loses lots of water via transpiration — a disadvantage in dry deserts. Tiny, waxy leaves minimise this water loss, which is crucial for survival there.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs a habitat correctly with its plant adaptation?
options: Desert — spines to reduce water loss
Mountain — broad leaves to catch snow
questions.explanation: Desert plants like cacti use spines to reduce water loss. Mountain plants use cone shapes (not broad leaves), plains plants don't need breathing roots, and oceans aren't matched with cone-shaped trunks.

questions.question: Deciduous trees like teak are adapted to plains by doing what during dry seasons?
options: Shedding their leaves to conserve water
questions.explanation: Deciduous trees like teak shed their leaves during dry seasons specifically to conserve water when it's scarce.

questions.question: A scientist finds a cold desert with very little rainfall but freezing temperatures. Based on the chapter's description of deserts, is this possible?
options: Yes, because deserts are defined by low rainfall, not just heat, and some deserts like Antarctica's are cold
No, deserts must always be extremely hot
No, deserts always have heavy rainfall
Yes, but only if it also has an ocean nearby
questions.explanation: The chapter specifically notes that deserts are defined by low rainfall, not high temperature — so cold deserts, like parts of Antarctica, do exist.

questions.question: What helps mango and neem trees stay green throughout the year?
questions.explanation: Mango and neem are evergreen trees that stay green year-round because they grow where water is consistently available.

questions.question: How does a pine cone's ability to open in dry weather and close in wet weather benefit the tree's reproduction?
options: It releases seeds when conditions favour dispersal and protects them when wet
It has no effect on reproduction
It only affects how tall the tree grows
It prevents the tree from ever making seeds
questions.explanation: Opening in dry weather lets seeds disperse (dry, windy conditions favour seed spread), while closing in wet weather protects the seeds from rot or premature germination — improving reproductive success.

questions.question: Which best describes 'plains' as a plant habitat?
options: Generally pleasant weather without extreme adaptation needs
questions.explanation: Plains generally have pleasant, moderate weather, so plants growing there usually don't need extreme special adaptations to survive.

questions.question: Mountain plants shed snow easily partly because of their cone shape.
questions.explanation: The cone shape of mountain trees like pine and fir helps snow slide off the branches rather than piling up and breaking them.

questions.question: Which is the key difference between an evergreen tree and a deciduous tree?
options: Evergreen trees stay green all year; deciduous trees shed leaves seasonally
Evergreen trees never grow tall; deciduous trees always grow tall
Evergreen trees only grow in deserts; deciduous trees only grow in mountains
questions.explanation: Evergreen trees (like mango, neem) keep their leaves and stay green throughout the year, while deciduous trees (like teak) shed their leaves during dry seasons.

questions.question: Why do cacti have spines instead of leaves? (Think about this from the chapter's opening question.)
options: Because leaves would lose too much water in the desert heat, while spines lose very little
Because spines help the cactus float
Because spines absorb more sunlight than leaves
questions.explanation: Broad leaves would lose too much water through transpiration in the hot, dry desert. Spines have a much smaller surface area, drastically reducing water loss.

questions.question: Adaptation allows plants to do what, in general?
questions.explanation: Adaptation allows plants to develop features that help them survive in the specific environment they grow in, whether desert, mountain, or wetland.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: Which plants have special roots that grow upwards to take in air in waterlogged soils?
questions.explanation: Mangroves have special breathing roots that grow upwards to take in air, allowing them to survive in waterlogged marshy soils.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: Why do coastal plants like coconut have waxy leaves?
questions.explanation: Coastal plants like coconut have waxy leaves to help conserve water in the often windy, salty coastal environment.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: What helps coconut trees withstand strong coastal winds?
questions.explanation: Coconut trees have flexible trunks that bend without breaking, which helps them withstand strong coastal winds.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: Why do grassland plants have deep roots?
options: To access underground water and prevent soil erosion
questions.explanation: Grassland plants have deep roots to reach underground water sources and help prevent soil erosion in open, often dry environments.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: Deep roots help grassland plants survive in open, dry environments.
questions.explanation: Grassland plants develop deep roots to access water stored deeper underground, which is essential for survival in open, often dry grassland environments.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: Why do forest trees typically grow tall and dense?
options: Due to abundant rain and sunlight
questions.explanation: Forest trees grow tall and dense because forests usually have abundant rain and sunlight, supporting rich, thick plant growth.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: Which forest tree is mentioned as having wide leaves to capture sunlight efficiently?
questions.explanation: Sandalwood is given as an example of a forest tree with wide leaves that help it capture sunlight efficiently in dense forests.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: Why do forest trees often need wide leaves, unlike desert or mountain plants?
options: Because dense forests can block sunlight, so wide leaves help capture more of it
Because forests never get any rain
Because wide leaves prevent all water loss
questions.explanation: In dense forests, sunlight can be blocked by taller trees, so having wide leaves helps a tree capture as much available sunlight as possible for photosynthesis.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: Why do mangrove roots being tangled and rising above the mud benefit the plant, in a marshy area?
options: They help the plant breathe and stabilize the muddy ground
They stop the plant from ever needing water
questions.explanation: Tangled mangrove roots rising above the mud let the plant take in air (since marshy soil lacks oxygen) and also help stabilize the loose, muddy ground.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: Which habitat is best associated with 'flexible trunks that withstand strong winds'?
questions.explanation: Coastal plants like coconut trees have flexible trunks specifically adapted to withstand the strong winds common along coastlines.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: Select ALL the adaptations associated with coastal plants like coconut.
questions.explanation: Coastal plants like coconut have waxy leaves (to conserve water) and flexible trunks (to withstand strong winds). Spines and cone shapes are adaptations of desert and mountain plants, not coastal ones.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: Marshes and swamps are typically waterlogged areas.
questions.explanation: Marshes and swamps have soil that is waterlogged, or saturated with water, which is why plants there (like mangroves) need special breathing roots.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: Why might grassland plants, despite having relatively simple-looking shoots, actually invest heavily in their ROOT systems?
options: Because grasslands are often dry, so deep roots are essential to reach water and hold soil
Because grassland plants never need sunlight
Because grassland plants have no shoots at all
questions.explanation: Grasslands are often open and dry, so plants invest in deep root systems to reach underground water and to anchor themselves and prevent soil erosion, even though their above-ground parts look simple.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: Which of these habitats is described as having 'abundant rain and sunlight', producing tall dense trees?
questions.explanation: Forests typically have abundant rain and sunlight, which supports the growth of tall, dense trees.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: What do mangroves (marshy areas), coconuts (coastal areas) and grasses (grasslands) all have in common in terms of adaptation focus?
options: They each adapt a specific part (roots, trunk, or root depth) to cope with their environment's main challenge
They all have spines instead of leaves
They are all classified as trees only
questions.explanation: Mangroves adapt their roots for air in waterlogged soil, coconuts adapt trunk flexibility for wind, and grasses adapt root depth for water and erosion control — each targeting their habitat's biggest challenge.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a coconut tree's waxy leaves?
questions.explanation: The waxy coating on coconut leaves helps reduce water loss, conserving water in the coastal environment.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: Sandalwood trees in forests use wide leaves to help capture sunlight efficiently amid dense tree cover.
questions.explanation: Sandalwood, growing in dense forests, uses wide leaves to maximise the sunlight it can capture even when overshadowed by other trees.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: Which habitat type is most associated with 'open, dry environments' and deep-rooted grasses?
questions.explanation: Grasslands are open, often dry environments where plants like grasses develop deep roots to find water and anchor against erosion.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: If a plant grows in a marshy area with roots poking above the muddy surface, what problem is it MOST likely solving?
options: Lack of oxygen in the waterlogged soil
Lack of any water at all
questions.explanation: Marshy, waterlogged soil has very little oxygen, so roots rising above the mud (as in mangroves) let the plant take in air directly, solving the oxygen shortage.

questions.topic: Marshes, Coastal, Grassland and Forest Habitats
questions.question: Which combination of habitats did the book group together as sharing certain plant adaptation themes?
options: Marshes and swamps, coastal areas, grasslands, and forests
questions.explanation: The book groups marshes/swamps, coastal areas, grasslands, and forests together as land and wetland habitats each requiring distinct plant adaptations.

questions.question: Which of the following is an aquatic plant?
questions.explanation: Lotus is an aquatic plant that grows in water, unlike pine, mango or cactus, which grow on land.

questions.question: How many broad categories of aquatic plants are described in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter describes three categories of aquatic plants: floating plants, fixed aquatic plants, and underwater plants.

questions.question: Which type of aquatic plants drift freely on the water's surface, not rooted in mud?
questions.explanation: Floating plants, like water hyacinth and duckweed, drift freely on the water surface and are not rooted in the mud below.

questions.question: Which of these are examples of floating plants?
questions.explanation: Water hyacinth and duckweed are floating plants — they drift on the water's surface without being anchored in mud.

questions.question: How do floating plants like water hyacinth stay afloat?
options: Their spongy stems act like life jackets
Their roots anchor deep in mud
They have no stems at all
questions.explanation: Floating plants like water hyacinth have spongy, air-filled stems that act like life jackets, keeping them light and afloat on the water.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the wide, flat leaves of floating plants?
options: To rest on the water's surface and soak up sunlight
questions.explanation: The wide, flat leaves of floating plants rest on the water's surface, allowing them to soak up sunlight for photosynthesis.

questions.question: Which plants are examples of 'fixed aquatic plants', anchored in the mud but reaching the surface?
questions.explanation: Lotus and water lily are fixed aquatic plants — anchored deep in the muddy bottom but with long stems that reach the surface.

questions.question: Why do fixed aquatic plants like lotus have long, hollow stems?
options: To stretch upward and push their leaves and flowers to the surface
To sink deeper into the mud
To store air only for animals
questions.explanation: Lotus and water lily have long, hollow stems that stretch upward from their muddy anchor point, pushing their leaves and flowers up to reach sunlight at the surface.

questions.question: Why does the lotus have a waxy coating on its broad leaves?
options: So water doesn't stick and cause the leaves to rot
So the flowers open only at night
questions.explanation: The waxy coating on lotus leaves keeps water from sticking, preventing the leaves from getting waterlogged and rotting.

questions.question: Which type of aquatic plants live completely underwater and absorb oxygen dissolved in the water?
questions.explanation: Underwater plants, like hydrilla and tape grass, live completely submerged and absorb oxygen dissolved in the water through their leaves, instead of breathing air.

questions.question: Which of these are examples of underwater plants?
questions.explanation: Hydrilla and tape grass are underwater plants that live completely submerged, with narrow leaves that sway with water currents.

questions.question: Why do underwater plants like hydrilla have soft, thin stems and narrow leaves?
options: To bend and sway with water currents without breaking
To grow the tallest of all plants
To capture the most sunlight above water
questions.explanation: Soft, thin stems and narrow leaves allow underwater plants like hydrilla to bend and sway with water currents instead of breaking under the water's movement.

questions.question: A plant has long hollow stems that reach the water surface. What type of plant is it?
questions.explanation: Long, hollow stems that reach the water surface while being anchored below describe a fixed aquatic plant, like lotus.

questions.question: In aquatic plants, __________ stems help them float on water.
questions.explanation: Spongy, air-filled stems act like life jackets, helping floating aquatic plants stay buoyant on the water's surface.

questions.question: Which common plant is described as an invasive species that can block sunlight in water bodies?
questions.explanation: Water hyacinth is a beautiful but invasive plant that can spread rapidly and block sunlight from reaching the water below.

questions.question: How can water hyacinth negatively affect aquatic life in a pond?
options: By reducing oxygen levels as it blocks sunlight for other plants
By adding too much oxygen to the water
questions.explanation: Water hyacinth can cover the water's surface, blocking sunlight from reaching submerged plants, which reduces photosynthesis and can lower oxygen levels, harming aquatic life.

questions.question: Besides being a problem plant, what useful product can water hyacinth be converted into?
questions.explanation: Water hyacinth, an invasive aquatic plant, can be converted into bioethanol, a clean fuel, helping put the problem plant to good use.

questions.question: Converting water hyacinth into bioethanol is described as an eco-friendly way to reduce pollution and save petrol.
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that turning invasive water hyacinth into bioethanol is an eco-friendly energy source that helps reduce pollution and reduce reliance on petrol.

questions.question: Which common floating plant is found in ponds and drifts freely without being rooted in mud?
questions.explanation: Duckweed is a common floating plant found in ponds, drifting freely on the surface without rooting in the mud.

questions.question: Why is duckweed sometimes removed from ponds?
options: To allow other plants enough sunlight and space
Because it produces too much oxygen
Because it has thorns that hurt fish
Because it makes the water too clean
questions.explanation: Duckweed can spread quickly and cover a pond's surface, so it is sometimes removed to allow other plants enough sunlight and space, keeping the ecosystem balanced.

questions.question: Managing plant growth, like removing excess duckweed, helps ensure what?
questions.explanation: Managing excess plant growth, such as removing duckweed, helps maintain a balanced ecosystem where all aquatic plants and animals can thrive.

questions.question: Floating plants easily get sunlight, while underwater plants don't get direct sunlight at the surface, yet both survive. What 'superpower' helps underwater plants cope?
options: They absorb oxygen dissolved in water and their leaves are adapted to use whatever light filters down
They have breathing roots like mangroves
questions.explanation: Underwater plants like hydrilla absorb oxygen dissolved in the water (rather than breathing air) and their thin, narrow leaves are adapted to use the filtered sunlight that reaches below the surface.

questions.question: Select ALL the plants that are classified as FLOATING plants.
questions.explanation: Water hyacinth and duckweed are floating plants. Lotus is a fixed aquatic plant (anchored in mud), and hydrilla is an underwater plant.

questions.question: Select ALL the plants that are classified as FIXED aquatic plants.
questions.explanation: Lotus and water lily are fixed aquatic plants, anchored in the muddy bottom with stems reaching the surface. Duckweed floats freely, and tape grass grows underwater.

questions.question: Which plant part of lotus and water lily rests on the water and helps collect sunlight?
questions.explanation: The broad leaves of lotus and water lily rest on or near the water's surface, helping the plant collect more sunlight for photosynthesis.

questions.question: Why do underwater plants like hydrilla not need to breathe air directly?
options: Because they absorb oxygen that is already dissolved in the water
Because they don't need oxygen at all
Because they have gills like fish
questions.explanation: Underwater plants absorb the oxygen that is dissolved in water through their leaves, so they don't need to reach the surface to breathe air.

questions.question: Which of these plants would you expect to have the LEAST need for a strong root system anchoring it to soil?
questions.explanation: Duckweed is a floating plant that drifts freely on the water's surface without roots anchored in mud, unlike lotus, mango trees, or grass, which all rely on rooting for stability.

questions.question: Which type of plant leaf shape is common among floating and fixed aquatic plants, to maximise sunlight capture on the water's surface?
questions.explanation: Floating plants (like water hyacinth) and fixed aquatic plants (like lotus) both tend to have wide, flat leaves that rest on the water's surface to capture sunlight.

questions.question: Aquatic plants have unique adaptations that help them thrive in water environments.
questions.explanation: Aquatic plants — floating, fixed, and underwater types — have each developed specific adaptations (like spongy stems, long stems, or narrow leaves) suited to life in water.

questions.question: What is the biggest overall lesson from comparing floating, fixed, and underwater plants?
options: Even within one habitat type (water), plants adapt very differently depending on their exact position relative to the surface
All aquatic plants are identical in structure
Only floating plants can survive in ponds
Underwater plants always grow taller than floating plants
questions.explanation: Floating plants (surface-drifting), fixed aquatic plants (rooted but reaching the surface), and underwater plants (fully submerged) show that even within the same broad habitat (water), plants adapt very differently depending on exactly where they live relative to the surface.
